newsitem.title: UK: UK firms' confidence at record high - survey.
newsitem.headline: UK firms' confidence at record high - survey.

text.p: Economic performance is strong and corporate confidence in Britain is at a record high, the UPS Europe Business Monitor survey published on Monday showed.

Some 40 percent of Europe's business leaders mentioned the UK as one of the countries which should show the strongest economic growth over the next three years. That is second only to Germany, which had been at the top for five years but has moved from fifth place to second in the last 12 months, the poll said.

Employment prospects across Europe have stabilized, but only in the UK do companies foresee a net increase in employment of three percent. Britain was the most "Euro-sceptic" country, with just 11 percent of the 1,500 surveyed feeling that European Union policies help employment at all. Some 31 percent said the EC was a hindrance in their competitive efforts in global markets.

The UK is the second most unpopular member of the EU after Greece (at 14 percent) with nine percent of European business leaders (mostly Belgians and French) wishing the UK was not a member, the survey, conducted in September and October, said.
Only two percent of British were against their own membership in the European Union.

British company leaders showed the weakest support for their own country's participation in the single currency after 1999 -- only 43 percent think it would be good for their company compared with 60 percent across the rest of Europe.
Only five percent of UK business leaders think the UK itself would join the EMU.
But UK companies are much more open to world markets, with only 37 percent compared with 49 percent in Europe overall looking to achieve most of their profit growth in Europe.

In the UK 60 percent are looking outside Europe, mostly to Southeast Asia (38 percent). However, their main selling efforts are towards Western Europe (53 percent) rather than Asia Pacific (21 percent).
A greater proportion of capital investments are to be concentrated in Western Europe (66 percent) with only 11 percent going to each of Asia Pacific and North America.

British business leaders are still the top supporters of concentrating on a core business rather than diversifying. They favor developing new foreign markets rather than focusing on the home market and are more likely to form strategic alliances than make acquisitions.
